part: die view: every die position (the logical map turned onto the die)
what_is_inferred: How the measured logical map sits on the die: logical x as die rows, y as die columns, memory shires 0-3 on the west, and the east-west sense (distances cannot tell a rotation from a mirror).
what_settles_it: Mostly settled by firmware source already in hand: the firmware's 'default Shire Virtual ID Map, based on the NOC spec' (noc_reconfigure.h:76-82), renamed by the boot firmware's NOC_Remap_Shires (main.c:284; 'No displacement' table noc_reconfigure.h:398-405, used when no shire is fused off), equals the measured map cell for cell with no rotation or mirror: 496 of 496 pair distances and 32 of 32 cells (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json). So the diagram's die view L34 is exactly the NoC-spec drawing: memory shires 0-3 on the left (west), PCIe then I/O at the right (east) end of the top row, as PRM Fig. 1-3 and datasheet Fig. 2-6 also draw it. Fact L37 ('does NOT match') compared the map before the renaming and is superseded. Still open: whether the silicon has this handedness or the published die plot's (I/O then PCIe, the mirror); a floorplan with labelled mesh stops, a die plot with its orientation stated, or the package ball map settles it.
ask_detail: top-level floorplan or an oriented, scaled die plot (AI Foundry); second source: the ET-SoC-1 Data Book / a final datasheet with the ball map

part: the four grey cells (master, spare, PCIe, I/O)
what_is_inferred: Which grey cell is the master shire (32), the spare (33), the PCIe shire and the I/O shire.
what_settles_it: Settled by the same firmware map (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json grey_cells): logical (0,3) = shire 32, the master (top row, die column 4); (5,3) = shire 33, the spare (bottom row); (0,4) = the bridge map's 'pcie0'; (0,5) = 'io0' (noc_reconfigure.h:84-90). This is L32's alternative reading (PCIe west of I/O, as PRM Fig. 1-3). To confirm on the cards: time SYSCALL_PMC_SC_SAMPLE on shire 32 from each compute shire (a + b x hops picks the top or bottom cell). E56 did so on 29 September (docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr, hub rung 31): on aifoundry1 card 1 shire 32 placed at (0,3), the firmware's cell (rms 1.1 cycles; the next cell, (0,4), 33.1); on aifoundry3 the calls' cost missed the frozen fit rule for a constant plus a term per hop (rms 4.7 cycles, at most 4 allowed), so the cell was not decided there, and the rule reports a place only when every card run agrees. PCIe/I/O order rests on the two firmware comments and the PRM; the NoC spec would confirm it.
ask_detail: exp-mesh-stops; the NOC spec that the firmware maps cite

part: memory shire placement (memory shire 2 a tie)
what_is_inferred: The memory shires' places come from a DRAM-latency fit on one card; memory shire 2's fit ties three places and is forced by elimination.
what_settles_it: The firmware map puts mc0-mc3 on the west at rows 1-4 and mc4-mc7 on the east at rows 1-4 (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-chip-diagram/research/firmware_map.json memshires): the fit's places for the 7 memory shires it places on its own, provided the firmware's mcN is the memory shire selected by PA[8:6] = N. With those 7 in place memory shire 2 has one cell left in both, so the map confirms the frame, not memory shire 2 on its own. What settles it on the cards: time SYSCALL_PMC_MS_SAMPLE (ms 0-7) from each of the 32 compute shires; each call's cycles are a constant plus a per-hop term to that memory shire, with no L3-home leg (the confound behind the tie). E56 did so on 29 September (docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr, hub rung 31): on aifoundry1 card 1 memory shires 0, 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 placed where the firmware map puts them, memory shire 2 at (3,-1), and 3 and 6 were not decided; on aifoundry3 nothing was decided (the calls' cost missed the frozen fit rule, as for the grey cells).

part: the four LPDDR4X packages (which two memory shires share each)
what_is_inferred: The pairing of memory shires to LPDDR4X packages (drawn as neighbours: 0+1, 2+3, 4+5, 6+7).
what_settles_it: The dev card's schematic: ET-PCIe-Dev-Card-V3.pdf p.1 links 'Schematic 09/27/2022', 'Board File V3.2' and the V3 schematic changes, none in external/et-man. Its block diagram (pdf p.4) and datasheet Fig. 2-6 both draw each LPDDR4X beside two neighbouring memory shires but number neither; the datasheet (pdf p.30) says only two memory shires per 64-bit device. No experiment identifies the package from software.
ask_detail: card schematic and board file (AI Foundry)

part: the mesh's routing order (every route the eleven flows draw)
what_is_inferred: Measured on 29 September (E56, fact L104): a request goes x first and its reply y first, back along the request's links; the diagram draws every route so (before, it drew every leg x first). Still inferred: which of a flow's packets travel as requests (TensorSend, TensorReduce and TensorBroadcast are drawn x first, like a store's data; E56 timed only tensor loads and stores), and the router-to-router flit width (L105 note).
what_settles_it: Settled for loads and stores by experiment: E56 ran sets of 1 KB tensor-load and tensor-store streams that share one directed link under one order and none under the other, frozen before the validation (tools/claims-v3/nocr/PREREG.md; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-nocr). On aifoundry1 card 1 and aifoundry3 the loads slowed only where their replies would share a link under y first, the stores only where their data would share one under x first, and a shared link carried about 92 GB/s. What is left: the same sets with TensorSend streams would place the tensor messages; the NoC configuration's generated reference manual (noc/reference_manual/noc_reference_manual.htlm, named at core-et rtl/inc/debug_defines.vh:831-832), the Main NoC documentation linked from CORE-ET Minion Shire Description §3.3 (pdf p.11, link missing) and the 'NOC spec' (noc_reconfigure.h:76, 84) would give the rule for every packet and the flit width. Interface: the routers' VC-status registers (noc_esr.h RIVCS/ROVCS), SP-only.

part: the way back of a DRAM load (Flow 1, Load -> DRAM)
what_is_inferred: The reply's path: the diagram draws it from the memory shire through the L3 home to the requester, each leg y first.
what_settles_it: The leg order is documented in a manual already in the repo: CORE-ET Shire Cache Specification §3.2.2 'L3 REQ_Read' (pdf p.55): L3 reads that miss go out the to_sys mesh port, the data returns to the L3 as L3_Fill, then the reply goes to the requester, so memory shire -> L3 home -> requester is spec. Each leg's route: a reply goes y first (E56, 29 September, fact L104), so the drawing takes each leg back along its request's links. What is left: E56's streams ran between compute shires' scratchpads, so that a memory shire's and an L3 home's replies follow the same rule is inferred.
ask_detail: cite the Shire Cache Specification; exp-route-order (E56) for the route of each leg

part: the inside of a shire (banks, neighbourhoods, UC block, mesh stop)
what_is_inferred: Where the four neighbourhoods, four cache banks, the UC block and the mesh stop sit in the 3.7 mm tile (the drawing is a block diagram).
what_settles_it: A minion-shire floorplan from the physical-design team. CORE-ET Minion Shire Description Figure 1 (pdf p.5) is logical; only the neighbourhood has a floorplan (Neighborhood MAS Figure 2, pp.7-8, already used by L115). No practical experiment: one temperature sensor per shire, and the crossbar may equalise bank latencies.

part: die sizes and the tile pitch
what_is_inferred: Die width and height and the hop length are pixel estimates on one die plot scaled to 570 mm2.
what_settles_it: The floorplan's dimensions (or the Data Book): die W x H, tile pitch, memory-shire strip width. The datasheet's package drawing (Fig. 9-1) has no die outline.

what_is_inferred: Was: 15.75 GB/s per direction, the Gen4 x8 link figure, with host transfers never timed.
what_settles_it: Settled on 27 September: timed on three cards with workloads/pciebench, five runs per card against predictions stated before the runs (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie; the page Over the PCIe link). Not a team ask.

what_is_inferred: Measured on 29 September (E55, fact pcie.write-l3): the host's writes go through their lines' L3 homes, which allocate the lines. After a staged 4 MB copy 99.5% of the lines read at L3 latency on aifoundry3 (99.9% on aifoundry1 card 1), whether the L3 held the buffer before or not, and no value read was stale. Still inferred, and drawn dashed: the L3's later write-back of those lines to the memory shires and DRAM.
what_settles_it: Settled by experiment: copy a buffer from the host, then time each line's first load in a kernel launched without the L3 flush; L3-hit latency means through the L3 homes (tools/claims-v3/pcie2/PREREG.md, frozen before the validation; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-pcie2). What is left: why the bridge sends the writes there. The PCIe shire's to-sys bridge has DRAM address-map entries for every shire's L3 slave (SHn_L3D) and for each memory shire (MC0..MC7_MEM) (etsoc-hal hwinc/noc_esr.h, BRIDGE_PS0_TOSYS ... MAP_MEM_DRAM), so the programmed ADBASE/ADMASK decide: read them (SP-only) or the NoC documents.

part: the DRAM address map below the memory shire
what_is_inferred: PA[9] channel, PA[12:10] bank, PA[34:18] row, decoded from firmware ADDRMAP values and a tool comment, and measured on 29 September (E57, fact L50): another row in the same bank conflicts, and a row that also differs in any of PA[6-12] reads as a row hit, on aifoundry1 card 1 and aifoundry3 (R33a); PA[6-9] set the refresh phase, so each controller refreshes on its own, on aifoundry3 (R33b; not established on card 1). Still open: whether two accesses on one controller serialise (R33c, insufficient on both cards).
what_settles_it: Settled for the banks and rows by experiment: single DRAM loads with every line evicted first, timed against the rows and banks the map predicts (tools/claims-v3/memp2/prereg/PREREG.md, frozen before the validation; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-memp2). What is left: the controller's serialisation (R33c's method did not resolve 6 cycles) and the refresh domain on a second card; a service-processor readback of each controller's ADDRMAP registers would settle the whole map.

part: the DRAM chip's share of a load (memory shire panel)
what_is_inferred: About 25-28 of a DRAM load's cycles are the DRAM's own timing; the rest on-chip (timing registers set against the fit).
what_settles_it: A memory-shire description with its pipeline latencies (NoC bridge, uMCTL2 controller, PHY, clock crossings) or a readback of the programmed DRAMTMG registers; or, as an experiment, DRAM latency at a second DRAM clock (needs a build: mem_controller.c:643 fixes 933 MHz; 800 and 1066 modes exist).

part: the tensor unit's cache path (tensor sequencer, L1 scratchpad)
what_is_inferred: Tensor loads skip the L1 but are cached in L2 and L3; tensor stores skip the L1 and L2 (energy manual; PRM confirms only the L1 bypass). The L2 part is measured (E57, 29 September): a second TensorLoad of the same 1 KB took 199 cycles, the L2 reference's 199, on aifoundry3 and aifoundry1 card 1. Not measured: whether the L3 keeps the lines, and the stores' bypass.
what_settles_it: Mostly documents already in the repo: CORE-ET Shire Cache Specification §3.5 'REQ_WriteAround' (pdf p.62): TensorStores issue writeArounds that bypass the L2 (coalesced in its buffer, written to the L3 or a remote scratchpad); Minion DCache Description: TensorLoad requests go out the L2 miss interface (pdf p.32) and fill the L1 scratchpad straight from the L2 interface (pdf p.41). Whether the L2 allocates tensor-load lines: settled by the re-load timing test (tools/claims-v3/memp2/prereg/PREREG.md, R36; docs/reports/data/2026-09-29-memp2). What is left: the L3's copy, by the same test with the L2 evicted between the loads, or shire-cache counters.
ask: document (in repo) + experiment (done for the L2)

part: the UC block, the I/O shire and the shire's voltage regions (one-line descriptions)
what_is_inferred: Not inferred, but thinly sourced: the UC block and the I/O shire's Maxions are drawn from one line of text, and the sources disagree on the Maxions' cache (4 MB in the datasheet and the PRM, 1 MB in the Shire Cache Specification).
what_settles_it: The design documents the open drop cites but leaves out: Power Spec, UC Specification, Shire Bus Master Specification, PLL/DLL Initialization, MAS: Minion Shire Debug, Debug High-Level Specification, Debug Memory Map, Minion CSRs, DFT Specification, Maxion Shire MAS, Maxion Tile MAS.

part: the host link's open questions (PCIe shire, Host, Flow 6)
what_is_inferred: Not inferred but unexplained, from the PCIe page: why two host-to-card DMA commands of one stream at once move half as much as one, and why card-to-host DMA dips at 32-64 MB per copy. E55 (29 September) found where the loss is: two commands in flight in one stream move 0.488 of one at 2 x 64 MB on aifoundry3, one command in each of two streams 1.012 (T35-S), and a shared read engine, the IOMMU, a fixed cost per overlap, a slow onset and a loss per element were refuted on both cards tested. aifoundry3's host copies memory at about half the others' rate because it runs one memory channel (docs/reports/data/2026-09-27-pcie/hosts.txt).
what_settles_it: What serves one stream's two commands in turn: the runtime's source for a stream's DMA queue, or the master minion's DMA worker in the firmware; the PCIe DMA engine's documentation, or the settings the firmware programs (channel arbitration, read-request size, element splitting), for the card-to-host dip; the lab admin's reads on the hosts (lspci -vvv for the payload and read-request sizes).
